newsitem.title: PERU: Peru '96 GDP seen boosted to 2.4-2.6 pct by fish.
newsitem.headline: Peru '96 GDP seen boosted to 2.4-2.6 pct by fish.

text.p: A bountiful year-end catch of anchovies and sardines gave Peru's economy an extra push last year, analysts said, and should notch up 1996 growth to between 2.4 to 2.6 percent.

Peru's economy picked up at the end of an otherwise sluggish 1996 and experts forecast the economy would forge higher this year, hitting growth of between 3.9 and 4.5 percent. Official data on 1996 growth is due out Tuesday.
GDP was only 2.2 percent between January and November of last year, a sharp slowdown from 7.0 percent throughout 1995.
Pablo Secada, macroeconomic analyst at local Santander brokerage, said a late surge in the fishing sector was the main factor behind the end-of-year snap-back.
"December was a good month, with (year-on-year) growth for that month expected at 7.2 percent, to give a total annual figure of 2.6 percent," he told Reuters.
"This growth was led by the fishing sector. There is an excess of capacity in this sector, so when you lift the fishing ban, as happened in this case, there is a rapid rise in the catch."
Secada predicted 3.9 percent growth for 1997, led by rises in mining, agriculture and construction.
"In the context of what happened in 1996 ... 2.6 percent overall growth is not so bad," he added, referring to the wooden pace of growth seen last year.

The government's forecast for 1996 is in the same ballpark as those of private economists, with officials targetting 2.5 percent. That outlook was scaled back considerably from an original five to six percent, as the economy plodded forward at its slack pace for most of the year. The administration is aiming for five percent growth in 1997.
Oscar Jasaui, head of the Lima economists' association and president of Duff & Phelps del Peru, agreed with the government's estimate of 2.5 percent 1996 growth.
Jasaui said the agriculture and fishing sectors led last year's growth, while the mining and industrial sectors would finish below the average, and construction would be negative.
"Construction depends on public spending and we all know that the government has tightened its belt," he said.
"For 1997, we think the GDP is going to rise four percent," he added.

Pablo Moreyra, analyst at ING Baring's Lima office, said he had fortified his original estimate of 2.4 percent growth for 1996 to 2.6 percent "due to a strong recovery in December of the fishing sector and also due to the agricultural sector, which had an excellent year."
He said agriculture, mining, and possibly also the financial sector, would spur growth of around 4.5 percent for 1997.

Ienzo Duarte, macroeconomic analyst at the local Apoyo consultancy firm, predicted 2.5 to 2.6 percent overall growth in 1996 due to an anticipated 7.3 percent to 7.5 percent year- on-year monthly rise in December.
"We estimate that this year growth will be four percent with a relatively good first quarter so as to enter the mid- year with a moderate growth rate," he added.
